name: Running pace
seoDesc: Running pace: work out speed from the time and the distance. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the time, the distance and the adjusted running pace and the Running pace calculator solves for speed. It is built for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Running pace calculator work?
sections.html:
The Running pace calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports speed in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the race distance (Previous race) and the units); then you type in the time, the distance (Estimate the finishing time for your next race) and the adjusted running pace.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Running pace calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Speed=distance ÷ time
Running pace=time ÷ distance
Your level (adjusted pace)=(compare to..., adjusted running pace, distance, race distance)
Predicted finishing time=(((race distance > 0) ? ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) ) : ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) )))
Distance=((((race distance > 0) ? ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) ) : ( (time, distance, compare to..., distance) )))) ÷ adjusted running pace
Table conversion=(((units) ? ( 621371 ÷ 1000000 ) : ( 1 )))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds
  • Run pace, opening in minutes:seconds per kilometer
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers

  • Run pace, opening in minutes:seconds per kilometer

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Running pace calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the time, the distance and the adjusted running pace — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Running pace calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns speed, derived from the time, the distance and the adjusted running pace. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Running pace calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the time, the distance and the adjusted running pace, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance (Previous race) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance (Previous race) opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 0 km. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Running pace calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
